entries.topicDescription: Choosing the right List, Set, and Map implementation and using them correctly.

tips.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList — the default should almost always be ArrayList
tips.content:
ArrayList is backed by a resizable array: O(1) random access,
amortized O(1) append, but O(n) insertion/removal in the
middle since later elements have to shift.

LinkedList is a doubly-linked list: O(1) insertion/removal
once you already hold a position, but O(n) random access
since reaching index i means walking i nodes from an end.

In practice, ArrayList wins almost every benchmark that isn't
a pathological "insert 100,000 times at the front" case — its
contiguous memory layout is far more cache-friendly than
LinkedList's scattered nodes, which usually dominates the
algorithmic difference. Default to ArrayList; reach for
LinkedList (or better, ArrayDeque) only when profiling says so.

tips.title: HashMap needs a correct hashCode()/equals() pair to work at all
tips.content:
HashMap locates a key's bucket using hashCode(), then uses
equals() to find the exact match within that bucket (in case
of collisions). If a key type overrides equals() without also
overriding hashCode() — or the two are inconsistent — lookups
silently fail: put() succeeds, but get() with an
equals()-equal key can return null because it lands in a
different bucket.

The contract is strict: if a.equals(b) is true, then
a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() must also be true. The reverse
isn't required (different objects can share a hash), but a
poor hashCode() that returns the same value for everything
degrades a HashMap to a linked list — O(n) lookups instead of
O(1).

Use records or an IDE-generated hashCode()/equals() pair
rather than hand-writing them; it's easy to get subtly wrong.

tips.title: List.of()/Map.of() return genuinely immutable collections, not just unmodifiable views
tips.content:
Collections.unmodifiableList(list) wraps a mutable list — the
wrapper itself rejects modification, but the underlying list
can still change out from under you if something else holds a
reference to it.

List.of(), Set.of(), and Map.of() (Java 9+) instead create a
truly immutable collection with no mutable backing store at
all. Any structural mutation — add, remove, set — throws
UnsupportedOperationException, and there is no way for the
contents to change later.

They also reject null elements outright (NullPointerException
on construction), which catches a class of bug earlier than a
regular ArrayList would. Prefer them for constants and method
return values you don't want callers accidentally mutating.
